questions.q: Why is isolating a critical production system described as a business-risk decision rather than a purely technical one?
options: Isolating a critical system can stop the attack while also taking the business offline, so the cost of that outage must be weighed, not just the technical action
Isolation is always technically impossible on production systems
Business-risk decisions never involve the security team at all
Isolating a critical system has no real downside, so the decision is trivial
questions.explain: Isolating a revenue-critical system stops the attacker but can also halt operations, which makes it a tradeoff between security and business impact.

questions.q: Which of these is NOT one of the factors described as going into a real isolation decision?
options: The analyst's personal preference for which tool to use
Confidence that the compromise is active and spreading
The business impact of taking the system offline
Whether a compensating control could reduce risk without a full outage
questions.explain: Real decisions weigh confidence, spread risk, business impact, reversibility, and compensating controls — not an analyst's personal tool preference.

questions.q: What is a compensating control, in the context of an isolation decision?
options: A narrower action, like blocking one port or disabling one account, that reduces risk without a full outage
A backup server that automatically replaces the compromised one
A requirement that isolation always be done twice
A tool that automatically isolates every system in the environment at once
questions.explain: A compensating control is a smaller, targeted action that can reduce risk when full isolation's cost isn't yet justified.

questions.q: Why do most real IR plans route high-impact isolation decisions through an authorization step rather than leaving it solely to the analyst?
options: Because the cost of a wrong call cuts both ways, and someone with authority to accept the business cost needs to make that call quickly
Because analysts are not allowed to use EDR tools under any circumstances
Because authorization steps have no real purpose and just slow things down
Because isolation decisions are never actually time-sensitive
questions.explain: The IR commander, CISO, or business owner carries the authority to accept the cost of either outcome, which is why they're brought into high-impact decisions.

questions.q: In the hospital vs. retailer example, why do the two organizations reach different decisions from the identical technical finding?
options: They're weighing genuinely different business realities — patient safety vs. peak-sales revenue — against the same security finding
The retailer's system was not actually compromised
The hospital's IR commander made an objectively wrong decision
Technical findings always produce the exact same decision regardless of context
questions.explain: The same technical finding can justify different decisions once the real business cost of containment is factored in — that's the whole point of the tradeoff.
